title: Optic flow based perception of two-dimensional trajectories and the effects of a single landmark.

findings.antecedent: complex manoeuvres (simulated optic flow)
findings.mechanism: optic flow provides information about rotation
findings.quote: Subjects appear to be capable to approximate the angle over which they are rotated, even during complex manoeuvres

findings.antecedent: linear+yaw stimuli (smaller rotations)
findings.mechanism: limitations in reproducing complex manoeuvres lead to overshoot for smaller rotations
findings.quote: overshoot for the smaller rotations

findings.antecedent: linear+yaw stimuli (large rotation, Ψo=360°)
findings.mechanism: limitations in reproducing complex manoeuvres lead to undershoot for large rotations
findings.quote: undershoot for the large rotation (Ψo=360°)

findings.antecedent: stimulus simulating no observer rotation
findings.mechanism: optic flow does not contain rotation information when no observer rotation is simulated
findings.quote: Yaw is never perceived when the stimulus does not simulate any observer rotation

findings.antecedent: stimulus with observer orientation fixed in environment (Ψo ≈ 0°)
findings.mechanism: clearer optic flow information when orientation is fixed in environment
findings.quote: Perception is close to veridical when orientation remains approximately fixed in the environment (Ψo ≈ 0°)

findings.antecedent: stimulus with observer orientation tangential to the trajectory
findings.mechanism: clearer optic flow information when orientation is tangential to the trajectory
findings.quote: and when it is tangential to the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: condition semicircle 90-turn
findings.mechanism: perception is close to correct when 0°≤|Ψo|≤|Ψp|
findings.quote: path rotation perception in condition semicircle 90-turn was not significantly different than in condition semicircle forward.

findings.antecedent: stimulus with |Ψo| ≤ |Ψp|
findings.mechanism: misattribution of yaw to path rotation leads to undershooting of path rotation
findings.quote: path rotation is, or tends to be, undershot when |Ψo| ≤ |Ψp|

findings.antecedent: stimulus with Ψo > Ψp (e.g., linear+yaw conditions where Ψp=0°)
findings.mechanism: misattribution of detected rotation (yaw) to path rotation
findings.quote: subjects seem to assume that the detected rotation results (mostly) from a rotation of the trajectory.

findings.antecedent: simulated yaw in opposite direction to trajectory rotation
findings.consequent: reports of straight paths or paths curving in wrong direction
findings.mechanism: misattribution of detected rotation (yaw) to path rotation
findings.quote: the number of reports of straight paths, or even paths curving in the wrong direction, increase with the presented Ψo.

findings.antecedent: condition semicircle half-counter (clockwise semicircle with counterclockwise half-turn)
findings.mechanism: strong misattribution of detected rotation (yaw) to path rotation causes perceived path to be straight
findings.quote: in condition semicircle half-counter... the average perceived path is more or less a straight line.

findings.antecedent: condition semicircle full-counter
findings.mechanism: strong misattribution of detected rotation (yaw) to path rotation causes perceived path to be a three-quarter counterclockwise arc
findings.quote: in condition semicircle full-counter, the average response is a three-quarter counterclockwise arc!

findings.antecedent: condition semicircle 64-counter (without landmark)
findings.mechanism: misattribution of detected rotation (yaw) to path rotation
findings.quote: This effect is already significant in condition semicircle 64-counter

findings.antecedent: condition semicircle 64-counter (with landmark)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional visual/extra-retinal information to disambiguate optic flow
findings.quote: but not when a landmark is present.

findings.antecedent: presence of a single salient landmark
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional visual information, extra-retinal information (from eye-movements), or a combination of both
findings.quote: The significant effects of the presence of such a landmark are shown in figure 5

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (in linear+yaw conditions)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional visual information, extra-retinal information (from eye-movements), or a combination of both
findings.quote: There are significant improvements in yaw and path perception for the linear+yaw conditions, when a landmark is present

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (in linear+yaw conditions)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional visual information, extra-retinal information (from eye-movements), or a combination of both
findings.quote: There are significant improvements in yaw and path perception for the linear+yaw conditions, when a landmark is present

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (short linear+yaw manoeuvre)
findings.mechanism: landmark improves perception of the ego-motion component that is relatively weak: translation (the path) in case of a short linear+yaw manoeuvre
findings.quote: The improvement of the perception of the path is largest for the short translations

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (long linear+yaw manoeuvre)
findings.mechanism: landmark improves perception of the ego-motion component that is relatively weak: rotation (yaw) in case of a long, otherwise identical manoeuvre
findings.quote: whereas the improvement in yaw is largest for the long translations.

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark
findings.mechanism: shifting landmark provides more dynamic visual information (parallax) or extra-retinal information (eye movements)
findings.quote: the errors are smaller for a shifting landmark than for a fixated one. These results are significant again for Ψo perception for the long translations

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark
findings.mechanism: shifting landmark provides more dynamic visual information (parallax) or extra-retinal information (eye movements)
findings.quote: and for Ψp for the short translations.

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (shifting or fixated) vs no landmark
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional visual/extra-retinal information to disambiguate optic flow
findings.quote: F(2,30)=4.58, p<0.0184; mostly due to the angular component)

findings.antecedent: fixated landmark
findings.mechanism: fixated landmark provides a stable reference point
findings.quote: the effect of the fixated landmark is the largest.

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (shifting or fixated) vs no landmark
findings.mechanism: landmark helps disambiguate optic flow, reducing illusory RIP percepts

findings.antecedent: presence of a fixated landmark (in semicircular conditions)
findings.mechanism: fixated landmark provides a stable reference point to aid yaw perception

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (when simulated manoeuvre had proportionally more yaw, i.e., short trajectory version)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional information to resolve ambiguity when yaw is high relative to translation
findings.quote: the perception of path rotation benefited more from the presence of a landmark when the simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally more yaw

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (when simulated manoeuvre had proportionally less yaw, i.e., long trajectory version)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional information to resolve ambiguity when yaw is low relative to translation
findings.quote: Perception of yaw improved more due to a landmark when the simulated manoeuvre contained proportionally less yaw

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (serving as reference point in semicircle inward conditions)
findings.consequent: number of responses excluded from analysis
findings.mechanism: landmark provides a stable reference point for movement perception
findings.quote: Much less responses to the conditions semicircle inward were excluded from analysis when the stimulus contained a landmark

findings.antecedent: adding a landmark (in majority of curvilinear conditions)
findings.mechanism: additional information was of no use or attention needed to interpret interfered with ego-motion perception
findings.quote: there was little effect of adding a landmark, and sometimes even a negative effect.

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark vs non-shifting landmark (in linear+yaw conditions)
findings.mechanism: shifting landmark provides more dynamic visual information (parallax) or extra-retinal information (eye movements)
findings.quote: the improvement of path rotation perception was bigger for a shifting landmark than for a non-shifting landmark.

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (in long linear+yaw translations)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional information to aid yaw perception
findings.quote: There is a significant increase in performance when a landmark is present for the long (large) translations.

findings.antecedent: presence of a single landmark (shifting or fixated) (in short linear+yaw trajectory stimuli)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional information to aid path perception, especially for short trajectories
findings.quote: There is a significant increase in performance when a single (shifting or fixated) landmark is present, due mostly to the effect on the perception of the small (short trajectory) stimuli (landmark/size interaction; p<0.03).

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark (in large linear+yaw translations)
findings.mechanism: shifting landmark provides more dynamic visual information to aid yaw perception in long translations
findings.quote: especially for a shifting landmark (p<0.035 for the large translations)

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark (any type)
findings.mechanism: landmark provides additional information to aid yaw perception
findings.quote: marginally significant over all responses

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark (in small linear+yaw conditions)
findings.mechanism: shifting landmark provides more dynamic visual information to aid path perception in short translations
findings.quote: Benefit is largest for a shifting landmark.

findings.antecedent: long linear+yaw translations
findings.mechanism: landmark presence improves yaw perception in long linear+yaw translations

findings.antecedent: shifting landmark vs no landmark
findings.mechanism: shifting landmark provides additional information to aid yaw perception
findings.quote: Landmark main effect, none vs. shifting F(1,5)=4.83; p<0.079

findings.antecedent: landmark type (none, shifting, fixated) in long linear+yaw translations
findings.mechanism: different landmark types provide varying degrees of information to aid yaw perception in long translations
findings.quote: Long, landmark main effect F(2,18)=4.06; p<0.0349

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark
findings.mechanism: landmark presence improves path perception
findings.quote: Landmark Main Effect; F(1,4)=12.28; p<0.0248

findings.antecedent: interaction between landmark presence and manoeuvre size
findings.mechanism: landmark effect on path perception is moderated by manoeuvre size
findings.quote: Landmark/Size interaction F(1,4)=12.17; p<0.0252

findings.antecedent: landmark type (none, shifting, fixated)
findings.mechanism: different landmark types provide varying degrees of information to aid path perception
findings.quote: Landmark Main Effect; F(2,14)=4.21; p<0.0370

findings.antecedent: presence of a landmark vs no landmark
findings.mechanism: landmark presence provides additional information to aid path perception
findings.quote: None vs. present: p<0.053

stimuli.description: Optic flow stimuli simulating linear or curvilinear 2D trajectories over a horizontal ground plane, with or without a single landmark (red dot attached to ground via blue dots). Landmarks could be shifting or fixated. Stimuli were 8s duration, preceded and followed by 2s stationary periods.

tables.description: List of simulated manoeuvre conditions, including trajectory type, observer orientation (yaw), size, and landmark presence/type.
Performance metrics (globally correct, trajectory correct, rotation in place) for each stimulus condition, including landmark types and number of responses.

limitations: The recorded reproductions did not always exactly match verbal descriptions, making it difficult to ascertain if the reproduction reflected actual perception or a categorization/sloppy response.
The good perception of yaw might partly be due to an observational/response strategy, as subjects tended to categorize rotations in steps of 90° or 180°.
The VR head-mounted display (VR4) had cushion distortion in the corners of its view, and the Datavisor LCD had a slightly different type of distortion.
Linear observer speed cannot be determined from optic flow alone without additional scaling information (e.g., knowledge of dot size).
